subtitle: The smallest tool with the biggest impact on your sound. Guitar picks affect your tone, attack, and playing comfort more than any other accessory.

introduction.title: What Makes a Guitar Pick?
introduction.text: A guitar pick is a small plectrum used to pluck or strum guitar strings. While seemingly simple, picks vary dramatically in material, thickness, shape, and texture, each affecting your playing style and sound in unique ways.

columns.title: Pick Anatomy
columns.text: Tip: The pointed end that strikes strings. Body: The grip area held between fingers. Shoulders: The curved sides for comfort. Bevel: The angled edge that contacts strings. Thickness: Measured in millimeters or gauge. Material: Affects tone and durability.

columns.title: Why Picks Matter
columns.text: Control attack and dynamics. Affect tone and brightness. Enable precise single-note playing. Provide consistent string contact. Allow faster playing techniques. Reduce finger wear and pain.

cards.title: Thin Picks (0.40-0.60mm)
cards.description: Flexible and bendable with a bright, crisp attack. Good for strumming but less control for single notes. Creates "pick noise" on strings and wears out faster.

fields.label: Best For
fields.value: Acoustic strumming, folk and country music, rhythm guitar parts, beginners learning to strum, light and delicate playing, open chord progressions

cards.title: Medium Picks (0.60-0.80mm)
cards.description: Balanced flexibility and control. Versatile for multiple styles and good for both rhythm and lead. Moderate attack and tone. Most popular thickness range with reasonable durability.

fields.label: Best For
fields.value: General purpose playing, rock and pop music, players switching between rhythm/lead, electric guitar, most beginner recommendations, versatile playing styles

cards.title: Heavy Picks (0.80-1.20mm)
cards.description: Rigid with minimal flex. Precise control and accuracy with warmer, fuller tone. Excellent for single notes with less string noise. Very durable.

fields.label: Best For
fields.value: Lead guitar and solos, jazz and fusion playing, metal and hard rock, fast technical playing, bass guitar (when applicable), precise articulation

cards.title: Extra Heavy Picks (1.20mm+)
cards.description: Very rigid with no flex. Maximum control and precision with thick, warm tone. Minimal pick noise. Can feel awkward initially but extremely durable.

fields.label: Best For
fields.value: Advanced lead playing, jazz and classical guitar, speed picking techniques, professional performance, specialized playing styles, players seeking maximum control

fields.label: Celluloid
fields.value: Classic plastic material, balanced tone. Most common pick material with good balance of flexibility and durability. Available in all thicknesses.

fields.label: Nylon
fields.value: Smooth, warm sound with good grip. Warmer tone than celluloid with excellent durability. Good for both acoustic and electric with less string noise.

fields.label: Tortoiseshell (Tortex)
fields.value: Synthetic alternative with excellent grip. Textured surface, consistent thickness and shape. Popular among professionals. Available in color-coded thicknesses.

fields.label: Horn & Bone
fields.value: Natural materials for vintage tone. Rich, warm tone character with smooth playing feel. Expensive but long-lasting. Preferred by some blues players.

fields.label: Eddie Van Halen
fields.value: Fender Heavy picks, precise attack for tapping

fields.label: James Hetfield
fields.value: Black Fender Heavy picks for powerful rhythm

fields.label: John Petrucci
fields.value: Jazz III picks for technical precision

fields.label: Brian May
fields.value: British sixpence coin for unique tone

cards.title: Storage Solutions
cards.description: Use pick holders, dispensers, or small containers to keep picks organized. Many guitar cases have dedicated pick storage compartments.

cards.title: When to Replace
cards.description: Replace picks when they show significant wear, chips, or rounded edges. Worn picks affect tone and playing precision.

cards.title: Emergency Picks
cards.description: Keep spare picks in multiple locations: guitar case, wallet, car, practice space. Consider stick-on pick holders for your guitar.

cards.title: Cleaning Tips
cards.description: Clean picks occasionally with soap and water. Some players sand pick edges for custom feel or use nail files to adjust worn tips.
